items.title: A fake Einstein quote actually explains the affordability crisis
items.summary: One of the most famous quotes commonly attributed to Einstein was something that he himself never actually said: “Compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world. He who understands it, earns it; he who doesn’t, pays it.” While the quote is not from Einstein at all, the math behind the concept of compound interest is incredibly profound, playing a role in any system — physical, mathematical, or financial — that accumulates based on how much of a base amount is present. When the base amount increases, it isn’t just the original amount (the principal) that continues to accumulate, but the additional amount (the interest) that adds to the accumulation as well. While investors most often use this to explain the growth of wealth in an interest-bearing account, it can be applied not just to wealth, but to the cost and price of goods and commodities that continue to increase over time as well. When wealth increases, we call it compound interest, but when prices increase, we call it inflation: not the cosmic kind , but the economic kind . The Einstein quote may be a fake, or at least grossly misattributed, but if you want to understand the current affordability crisis, the mathematics and the concept behind the quote is exactly what everyone should understand. Here’s how it works. This image shows Albert Einstein playing his violin in 1932. While Einstein had a great many famous quotes and sayings over his life, there is no evidence he ever remarked anything about compound interest, or called it “the greatest invention” or the “eighth wonder of the world” or anything of that ilk. It appears that was an invention of a New York Times writer from 1983. Credit: Bettmann Collection / Getty Images The story behind the quote Einstein grew to fame in the early 20th century, and died in 1955. While an enormous amount of his writings, speeches, and interviews survive, nothing that he ever said or wrote relating to compound interest survives. The earliest assertion that the quote was said by Einstein can be traced back to a 1983 New York Times column , which mentions the quote as a popular saying that’s attributed to him. But it’s likely that the attribution was made up entirely, as there is no print record of the quote — or any saying linking Einstein to the concept of compound interest — prior to that. An investigation into the quote’s origins unearthed two very similar statements that may provide the ultimate inspiration for the eventual saying that became linked with Einstein’s name. In 1916, a newspaper advertisement in California described compound interest as “the greatest invention the world has ever produced.” A little bit later, in 1925, the phrase “the eighth wonder of the world is compound interest” was used by a Cleveland savings and loan company. It is unknown what sort of intersection of: fabrication, marketing by financial firms looking for investment, and antisemitic thoughts (about the link between Einstein, Jews, and banks), played a role in conferring an Einsteinian attribution to the actual quote itself. This height by age chart, published in 2000 by the CDC, shows a roughly linear growth in height in boys from the age of 2 until adulthood. There is no compounding in humans when it comes to increases in height; the increase comes instead in a linear fashion. Credit : CDC The math of compound interest When most of us think of growth, we think of what’s known as linear growth: where things grow by a given amount over a given interval. If you have a child and the child grows by 7.6 centimeters (3 inches) per year, then a baby who’s initially born at 51 centimeters (20 inches) will, after 17 years, have grown to a height of 180 centimeters (5 feet 11 inches). In linear growth, the amount that you gain does not depend on the amount that you already have. Instead, the growth is by a fixed amount over a given time. Financially, it would be like getting $100 every year on your birthday: after 17 years, you would have $1700. On the other hand, compound interest accumulates based on the base amount that you already have. If you accumulate interest at a 4% rate annually, then if you start with $100, how much will you have after 17 years? You might think — and this is incorrect, linear thinking — that you should just multiply that 4% by 17 years, giving you 68%, growing your $100 to $168. But the way compound interest works is different. For the first year, you earn 4% interest on $100, giving you $104. For the second year, you earn 4% interest on $104, giving you $108.16. For the third year, you earn 4% interest on $108.16, giving you $112.49. For the fourth year, you earn 4% interest on $112.49, giving you $116.99. And so on. Note that for each year beyond the first, you don’t just gain $4 a year (the 4% of the initial $100), but more than $4, as you get 4% interest on the full amount of your balance. By the time a full 17 years have elapsed, your initial $100 will have grown to $194.79: a significant increase over the $168 you’d expect with linear growth. The idea of compound interest is that instead of just gaining the same amount year-after-year on your initial investment, the interest that you earn gets re-invested alongside the principal, where they both earn interest together. Over long periods of time, this can add up to a tremendous advantage over “linear” interest and growth alone. Credit : Pixy/CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 There are three factors that matter when it comes to compound interest. The first is simple: the rate of growth, known as the interest rate. If we took that same analysis — starting with $100 and growing it for 17 years — but upped the interest rate to 5%, 7%, or 9%, that initial investment would instead have grown to $229.20, $315.88, or $432.76, respectively after those 17 years elapsed. The second is also simple: the duration of time of the investment. If we go back to that original 4% interest rate, but consider longer-term investments, we can see how continued growth helps increase the amount that you gain. If you wait 30 years, 50 years, or (generationally) 250 years, your initial $100 would grow to $324.34, $710.67, or $1,812,737.11, respectively, at that same 4% rate. Time makes an enormous difference when it comes to compound interest, especially over the long run. The third is a little more complicated: how often the interest is compounded. In the prior examples, we compounded the interest annually: we calculated the interest based on how much we had as the principal amount at the start of the year, and then added the interest to the balance at the end of the year, where it becomes part of the new principal. After 17 years, if we compounded the interest quarterly, monthly, or daily, then instead of $194.79, we’d have $196.72, $197.16, or $197.38. All three of these factors matter for the same underlying reason: interest gives you growth, and the amount of growth you get is determined by both the interest rate and the principal amount. When you grow the principal, you get interest not just on the original balance, but on the “amount of growth” too, and this accumulates over time. This graph shows the difference of a 20 year investment that accrues 10% in simple interest per year (gaining 10% of the original principal value, annually) versus 10% compounding interest, where after each year, the interest is added back into the principal and begins accruing interest as well. The greater the amount of time that passes, the more the two curves depart from one another. items.title: Six Books You Should Read Twice
items.summary: In the seven years I taught writing to first-year university students, I always began the semester the same way: We’d start with lessons on how to read critically. To help them, I introduced the concept of the hermeneutic circle—a fancy philosophical name for a simple idea. To comprehend the meaning of a book, readers need to analyze its individual sentences and paragraphs, but those parts can’t be interpreted without understanding how they work as a whole. In practice, this usually means reading to the end and going right back to the beginning. The hermeneutic circle isn’t just for academics, though; it explains why some novels feel impossible to put down. You’re using it when you flip back to the opening of a mystery after you’ve reached a pivotal scene that changes what you thought you knew. Sometimes a plot twist completely flips your understanding of a character, and you can’t help but reread the novel, this time with your eyes wide open. The six books below feature unreliable narrators, jarring perspective shifts, and slow-burning reveals. As soon as they’re over, they demand to be instantly started again. Devil House , by John Darnielle Darnielle, the front man for the indie band the Mountain Goats, starts his third novel simply enough. Gage Chandler, a once-acclaimed true-crime writer, is sniffing out what just might be his next hit: an investigation into a 1986 unsolved double murder at a former porn shop. Some 20 years later, Chandler has moved into the scene of the crime, dubbed “Devil House,” to immerse himself in the story. But the more time he spends going through grisly source material purchased from eBay, the more he chafes at his task. Then Darnielle takes Devil House down a series of sharp left turns, and each new section feels like its own book: This meta-novel grows to include the story of the crime that inspired Chandler’s debut, The White Witch of Morro Bay , and a faux–Middle English myth rendered in Gothic font. Darnielle’s eventual return to Devil House—and Chandler’s accounting of the costs of digging up its history—is no less surprising. The reader is left to reassemble this dissection of the true-crime genre, and then to ponder what it means to arrange jumbled puzzle pieces into a coherent portrait. [ Read: 15 books you won’t regret rereading ] Dirtbag, Massachusetts , by Isaac Fitzgerald Though his memoir-in-essays is subtitled A Confessional , and though it opens by revising the story he and his family used to tell about his childhood, Fitzgerald doesn’t immediately lay bare the lingering pain of his tumultuous upbringing. The first 11 essays are plenty vulnerable: Fitzgerald writes that he was born of an affair; spent his early years living in a homeless shelter and then in low-income housing run by the Catholic Worker movement; moved to north-central Massachusetts, where “violence was the solution, problem, and consequence”; and began abusing alcohol and drugs before age 13. But these are mere “flashes of the past,” as Fitzgerald writes in the last essay, “My Story,” where he takes full control of the narrative of his life. As he admits to having avoided the full truth, Fitzgerald becomes his own confessor, the one with the power to forgive. Drive Your Plow Over the Bones of the Dead , by Olga Tokarczuk, trans lated by Antonia Lloyd-Jones Janina Duszejko, the strange older woman who narrates this Nobel Laureate’s fairy tale–tinged noir thriller, seems too caught up in her devotion to animals, astrology, and the poetry of William Blake to involve herself in anything as petty as a whodunit. But when poachers start turning up dead in Duszejko’s remote Polish hamlet in the Kłodzko Valley, she fights to make the police listen to her theory of the crimes: The animals who have long made their home in the village’s bordering forest are taking their revenge. In Tokarczuk’s hands, Duszejko is no “crazy madwoman,” as the police see her, but a prophet—the only one who can see that “animals have a very strong sense of justice.” On a second pass, with full knowledge of why Duszejko becomes so wrapped up in the murder investigations, you can better appreciate how Tokarczuk subverts the thriller’s typical form with a philosophical meditation on how humans have become all too comfortable with destroying the natural world. [ Read: The case for rereading the high-school classics ] Loved and Missed , by Susie Boyt I picked up Loved and Missed after seeing it recommended again and again by fellow critics as a touching, engrossing novel about the pleasures of caregiving , one that they were desperate to talk about. The book—largely narrated by a middle-aged schoolteacher named Ruth as she takes over the parenting of her granddaughter, Lily, from her drug-addicted daughter, Eleanor—is indeed poignant and charming. Ruth builds a cozy home life after deciding that Lily “was not going to have a poultice childhood, a mending service, scrappy and provisional.” Yet buzzing beneath this domestic bliss is the live wire of Eleanor’s presence and absence, and the reader is forced to wonder how Lily is affected by being the object of all of Ruth’s displaced motherly love. Then, in the last chapter, Boyt hands the reins of narration to the teenage Lily, adding a fresh charge to all that came before. No wonder we can’t stop talking about it. She’s Under Here: A Love Story, a Horror Story, a Reckoning , by Karen Palmer The first time I read Palmer’s memoir of fleeing her abusive ex-husband and assuming a new identity, I hardly came up for air. I was fully submerged in her recounting of 14 dangerous years of marriage—including a harrowing scene of her ex holding a gun to her pregnant belly—followed by escalating torment after she flees with her daughters. But this memoir of surviving domestic violence and then coming to terms with what it costs to start over entirely, including forged birth certificates and a fake life story, deserves to be lingered over, just as Palmer’s fear stayed with her for decades. Only on my second read, once I had made it through with Palmer to safer shores, was I able to fully appreciate the author’s persistent doubts about the choices she was forced to make, as well her haunting meditations on why she stayed for so long. [ Read: What rereading childhood books teaches adults about themselves ] Women and Children First , by Alina Grabowski The fictional decaying coastal town of Nashquitten, Massachusetts, is a place where “it seemed like there was a death every month”—opioid overdoses, drunk driving, suicides. But the mysterious death of the aspiring artist Lucy Anderson at a high-school party stands out. Grabowski follows the ripples and rifts that led to and came after Lucy’s demise via a Rashomon -like structure, switching among the perspectives of 10 different girls and women connected to Lucy: her classmate, her guidance counselor, her best friend, her mother. Each narrator’s story offers a shard of what happened at that party, yet their points of view are contradictory and hopelessly biased, each coloring the reader’s understanding of what came before. Women and Children First is less a puzzle than a kaleidoscope, offering several misaligned but interconnected visions of the truth. The satisfaction comes not from any definitive reveal of what happened to Lucy, but from unraveling how all these characters’ actions and stories affect one another—something you can only really understand once you’ve finished the book and gone back to page one.

items.title: Catapult Is Closing Down, but the Work Lives On
items.summary: If you’re tapped into the indie publishing world, you may have heard last week about the dissolution of cornerstone Catapult Books . After 10 years of helping emerging writers find footing in a turbulent literary ecosystem, Catapult announced it would cease operations by the end of the month. Neither current employees nor the union, the Catapult Workers Collective, will transfer to the new buyer, and until recently, it was unclear what would happen to the forthcoming titles for Spring 2027. Despite fears, we’ve confirmed that all the Catapult Group’s forthcoming titles will still be released as planned. It’s an unpredictable and disturbing time to navigate literary publishing. It certainly feels worth noting that the company was sold while the Catapult union was on the brink of contract bargaining, and that union members were notified that continued employment was “ not an option .” The sale of Catapult raises concerns for authors and publishing professionals alike, and there’s no doubt that Catapult’s absence from the independent publishing landscape will be keenly felt. Now that the Spring 2027 titles have been confirmed, we feel it’s more important than ever to share these books. Pre-ordering is a great way to show support for these authors, and to affirm our continued need for the kind of valuable work Catapult was doing in the literary landscape. –Lennie Roeber-Tsiongas Assistant Editor Untranslatable by Lara Vergnaud Untranslatable is an “irresistible, razor-sharp memoir about a literary translator’s many selves—artist, mother, global citizen—as she navigates the strange convergences of family and work, life and craft.” Elisabeth Jaquette, who translated Minor Detail , calls it “a gift to anyone who cares about language, love, and how the stories that shape us are told.” A Handful of Arrows by María Gainza, translated by Thomas Bunstead The author of Optic Nerve and Portrait of an Unknown Lady is back with a genre-bending collection exploring how “works of art move both through the physical world and our cultural imaginations.” Adam Thirlwell calls it “an inside-out novel about memory and forgetting that will leave every reader disturbed, enriched and delighted.” The River Drowns the Able Swimmer by Xujun Eberlein This memoir spanning from the end of the 19th century into the present is a multi-generational story following Eberlein’s grandmother, mother, and herself “as they define themselves against a backdrop of China’s turbulent history” and “struggle to build a life of one’s own amid the perturbations of capital-H history.” Rose by Oksana Vasyakina, translated by Elina Alter Rose is the third book in Vasyakina’s trilogy, this time telling the story of an autofictional Vasyakina attempting to understand the story behind her aunt’s life and death that explores “lineage . . . the intimacy, pain, and resilience that define womanhood in a patriarchal world.” The Vanishi n g Act by Eoin Connolly Eoin Connolly’s The Vanishing Act is “part apocalyptic satire, part cri de coeur for our overwhelmed nervous systems.” The novel follows a “socially inept” copywriter named Colm whose climate-anxiety leads him make the decision to vanish “first from the Internet and then completely.” Best Debut Short Stories 2026 edited by Kendall Storey and Elizabeth Pankova Featuring the winners of the 2026 PEN/Robert J Dau Short Story Prize for Emerging Writers, this anthology celebrates new voices in literature. The Ruiners by Ellena Savage Described as a “sharp, funny, and deeply felt consideration of global capitalism and its misdoings,” Ellena Savage’s debut novel follows 29-year-old Pip and her new boyfriend, Sasha, after Pip spends her inheritance money on a falling-apart house on an “environmentally ravaged” island in Greece. The Rootless Elysium by Aatish Taseer A “meditation on migration, identity, and the fragile idea of America as a ‘creedal nation,’” Taseer’s The Rootless Elysium follows Taseer on a Route 66 road trip that grows into something much more. As Taseer journeys across America, he “confronts the competing seductions of rootlessness and rootedness, the persistence of race and history beneath a myth of new beginnings, and the uneasy realization that exile is no longer temporary.” Notes on Postcards by Jennifer Croft Jennifer Croft’s new memoir is an exploration of “ wanderlust, love, and motherhood seen through a lifelong collection of postcards . . . posing fundamental questions about why and how we connect to each other, to our histories and geographies, our languages, pictures, and ourselves.” Jealousy by Sarah Haas “An obsessive, propulsive memoir” about, as the title suggests, jealousy. Haas follows the path of jealousy throughout a relationship and across “art, myth, photographic technology, and perception.” A personal story that opens into fascinating questions about the broader culture, the book asks: “What if the only way to understand ourselves is to embrace jealousy? To admit it as a part of the self—even if the worst, most despotic part—and then to honestly describe and so face it.” Doppelgänger by Sam Riviere Riviere’s Doppelgänger is a “hilarious, scathing, and absurdist critique of contemporary culture set in a fictional university town in the near future where a contagious ‘twinning’ trend has swept across the student body.” Readers will ask: “Is this a scathing critique of contemporary culture or a virtuoso game of cat and mouse? Who’s to say? A bit of both, probably.” On Another Planet They Can Save Me by Lieke Marsman, translated by Sophie Collins When poet and novelist Lieke Marsman was diagnosed with a rare type of bone cancer in 2017, she was told it was incurable. On Another Planet They Can Save Me follows an “intellectual journey that challenges the limits of the rational, secular worldview she once trusted. As she undergoes radiotherapy, immunotherapy, and multiple surgeries—including the amputation of her arm—[Marsman] turns to theology, philosophy, mythology, and science in an urgent quest for hope.” Cloud Six by Amy Fusselman Amy Fusselman’s Cloud Six follows a couple who, after dying in a plane crash, find themselves on the “lowest tier of heaven, filled with laughter and dread, fear and acceptance, and family bonds even death can’t break.” Cloud Six offers “a blistering yet humorous take on the many trials of contemporary life, including parenting, substance abuse, depression, gun violence, and climate change.” The Birthing Tree by Amanda Peters From the author of The Berry Pickers comes a new “unforgettable novel about a woman who must confront her family’s buried truths and memories of passionate young love when her grandmother’s death leaves her as the only guide to her community’s future.” The Birthing Tree is a “sweeping yet intimate novel [that] follows one woman’s journey to protect the land, the traditions, and the memory of the women who came before her—and to decide which parts of her inheritance she will carry into the future.” The Loneliest Tree in the World by Mariana Salomão Carrara, translated by Julia Sanches and Alison Entrekin The Loneliest Tree in the World is a “whimsical novel by a beloved Brazilian writer [that] follows a family of tobacco farmers through the eyes of various objects in their home—an old mirror, a pickup truck, a protective work smock, and a sick, loving tree.” Translated by Julia Sanches and Alison Entrekin, “Mariana Salomão Carrara experiments with language and form to portray a family in crisis.” Replace Me by Amber Husain Amber Husain’s Replace Me is “a bold and engrossing exploration of replacement—professional, romantic, and political—and the anxiety it stokes in our ever-shifting cultural landscape.” Considering the widespread fear of employment obsolescence in the age of AI, Husain asks: “

items.title: Mapping the brain won’t unlock all its secrets. That’s a good thing.
items.summary: There’s a quote attributed to New Zealand physicist Ernest Rutherford that goes something like this: “All science is either physics or stamp collecting.” In other words, some scientists perform experiments to explain how things work, while others don’t test specific hypotheses but instead observe the natural world and take note of what they find. The latter may seem inferior, but don’t underestimate the influence of observational science; after all, biology’s greatest stamp collector was probably Charles Darwin, who planted the seeds of his theory of evolution by natural selection in his detailed field journal published in 1839: The Voyage of the Beagle . In neuroscience, two types of stamp collections — wiring diagrams, or connectomes , and parts lists, or cell type atlases — are a major focus of time, effort, and financial investment. For example, the adult Drosophila connectome, published on a website called FlyWire.ai , is freely available for anyone to peruse. Upon its announcement, neuroscientist Sebastian Seung proclaimed in the New York Times that “mind uploading” had hit the mainstream. The entire connectome, minimized to fit my computer screen, looks a bit like the tangled mess I pull out of my hairbrush every morning, except that each strand is color-coded to ease tracing its long, thin processes throughout the structure. Apparently, at least according to Seung, I’m staring at an uploaded mind. But what does it actually tell me? One is immediately struck by the sheer number of neurons and connections. It’s humbling, given that when I started as a student of neuroscience, I would blindly record from spiking neurons, one by one. It felt like trying to understand a whole planet full of people by speaking to one random person at a time. The connectome is a resource, but in and of itself it is not a specific answer to a specific question. Though it took an enormous amount of time, effort, and money to generate it, it’s not necessarily clear what breakthroughs will come of it and what those discoveries will mean for either basic science or human health. But does this matter? Until recently, the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans was the only organism for which a complete or near-complete connectome existed. Each of its 302 neurons is labeled, studied, and identified. The first draft of the C. elegans connectome was published by South African biologist Sydney Brenner and colleagues in 1986. Brenner, who started studying the species in the mid-1970s and championed it as a model, received a Nobel Prize in 2002 for his work in the role of genetics in its organ development. Fittingly, his Nobel lecture was titled “Nature’s Gift to Science” — an homage to the tiny worm and the value of selecting the appropriate model organism. Like other model organisms, C. elegans offers many practical benefits to a lab beyond its 302-neuron nervous system. It is one of the smallest and simplest organisms that is nevertheless multicellular (the fruit fly’s body, for example, comprises over half a million cells, while C. elegans has about 1,000 in total), and it is easy to maintain in bulk populations. Like other roundworms, C. elegans does not have blood or a respiratory system. It does, however, have an intestine and well-studied muscular structure. It is small — about one millimeter in length as an adult — and a large number of individuals can be kept in a single petri dish lined with agar, a jellylike substance commonly used in the lab to grow bacteria. The worms are remarkably sturdy creatures and can be purchased and stored easily in the freezer until they are thawed for use in experiments. They are particularly useful for research into the roles of genes in development, since their small number of cells are easy to track over their lifespans. On that last point, aging is a big topic of research in the species, as its lifespan of about two weeks is conveniently short. C. elegans is also one of the simplest and smallest organisms that nevertheless has a nervous system and exhibits complex behaviors such as thermotaxis (movement toward temperature cues), chemotaxis (movement toward chemical cues), and mating, among others. It is the most primitive organism known to exhibit a lethargic state comparable to sleep, and when exposed to nicotine, it exhibits some of the classic features of addiction, like withdrawal. The C. elegans connectome was generated using painstaking anatomical methods — essentially, slicing the microscopic worm into thin sections and imaging its cells using a powerful, high-resolution technique for preserved tissue called electron microscopy. More complete versions or variations of the worm’s connectome were published in the decades after Brenner’s initial version. But it’s important to note here, in a truth at once frustrating and humbling, that neuroscientists still don’t fully understand how the C. elegans nervous system works despite having had a complete wiring diagram of it for decades. One of the major reasons for this is that the living nervous system, even in a worm, can behave differently — more dynamically and flexibly — than its static wiring diagram would suggest. To be fair, FlyWire gives us a lot of additional insight beyond showing connections. The Drosophila connectome it shows is not just a static map but a highly interactive and searchable database that scientists can use to quickly glean almost everything there is to know about their neuron, or brain region, of interest. We can compare the connectomes from male and female individuals, as well as from an adult brain and a larval brain, to understand how different cell types and connectivity patterns emerge throughout development or support sex-specific behaviors. But if there’s anything we’ve learned from connectome projects thus far, it’s that stamp collections of the brain’s cells, chemicals, and connections, as comprehensive as they are, raise far more questions than answers. Take, for example, the work of neuroscientist Eve Marder from Brandeis University. Marder spent years researching the crustacean stomatogastric ganglion (STG) — a small circuit of about 30 neurons that generates rhythmic movements in a crustacean’s digestive system in response to food, in order to move it along the digestive tract and break it down. Her work, dating back to the 1990s, shows that even with a relatively simple circuit that produces a well-defined behavior, understanding the role of each neuron and each connection is anything but straightforward. One thing I’ve learned as a scientist, however, is that stamp collections like the connectome are worthy for precisely these reasons: They don’t give us the answers, but they help us to ask the right questions. One major reason for this is that even in small circuits, neurons are highly interconnected in complex ways. For example, though a connectome can show synaptic connections between two neurons, scientists also need to know what type of connection it is: Neurons can exchange either chemical or electrical signals across synapses, and in some cases two neurons can share both types of connections. Neurons also can inhibit each other or be connected both directly and indirectly via other neurons, making their ultimate behavior in the circuit very hard to predict. Circuits that govern two different behaviors — in the case of the lobster STG, two different digestive movements — are not neatly segregated. A neuron’s role therefore can’t be neatly categorized by which circuit or behavior it participates in. Finally, environmental conditions like temperature can impact the timing at which neurons fire and thus the downstream consequences of their activity. All of this suggests that though we can see wiring patterns in a connectome, we can’t necessarily tell which connections are important and under what conditions. items.title: How your brain’s hemispheres actually work
items.summary: Neuropsychiatrist Iain McGilchrist has spent over three decades studying how the brain’s two hemispheres shape consciousness, and says almost everything we think we know about them is wrong. The “logical left, creative right” story that took hold in the 1980s and ’90s was never accurate. McGilchrist traces this back to a basic survival problem — how to eat without being eaten — and argues the right hemisphere’s mode of understanding, grounded in context and nuance, gets us closer to reality than the left’s ever can. This video How your brain’s hemispheres actually work is featured on Big Think .

items.title: TELEVISION Walks the Tightrope Between Reality and Performance
items.summary: In Television , Lauren Rothery’s debut novel, the narrative switches between the interior monologues of Hollywood hopefuls, mainly Verity and Helen. Forever friends, sometimes lovers, they come to Los Angeles separately but for the same reason: to escape from somewhere else. Hollywood, however, is not sentimental about origins; it is a sorting machine. Some make it. Some don’t. Verity makes it—spectacularly. Helen does not. Verity is, we are told, very attractive. Helen, less so. The question that haunts Verity is whether it’s his tremendous good looks or his talent that accounts for the difference in their success. In an attempt to balance the cosmic ledger, to correct what he sees as the unfairness of his outsized success, Verity creates a lottery to give away his multi-million dollar salary from his acting role in the latest blockbuster. Rather than absolving him, the gesture only makes Verity more famous. Through it all, Verity and Helen are bound by something rare: a mutual understanding of each other that feels singular. Yet even this intimacy warps under the pressure of Verity’s success. At one point in the novel, in a gesture that reads as both romantic and obsessive, Verity buys the apartment complex where Helen lives and moves into the unit next door. Like many successful actors, Verity is most himself when he is playing a role, and with Helen he is able to play house. Here, Rothery captures the uncanny position of the actor in relation to life: Performance can feel truer than sincerity. As a result, what emerges for both Verity and Helen isn’t a domestic life but its occasional simulation—an arrangement perpetually on the verge of collapse, as if a closer inspection of their surroundings might reveal it to be a film set, all pasteboard frontages, plywood facades, and painted-on windows. Such is the sensation of reading Television : the feeling that the novel itself might dissolve in your hands. Rothery’s sly prose slips across the boundary between reality and performance so that nothing escapes the sense of feeling staged, suggesting that Hollywood does not simply reward acting—it makes actors of us all. Lauren Rothery and I spoke over Zoom about celebrity, luck, and the myth of meritocracy in the arts. Television will be released in paperback on November 3. Evander James Reyes: How did you arrive at the title Television ? Lauren Rothery: It was the title from really early on—it just felt right. It ended up connecting to a number of different things in the book. There’s the industry shift from film into television and streaming. And then there’s that moment near the end when Verity talks about what he finds romantic about television—an older version of it that I’m not sure exists so much anymore—where you really fall in love with a set of characters and just keep wanting to hang out with them. It’s not about the plot. You just want to be around them. EJR: The novel does feel structured like a classic television show in that way. We tune in to the lives of these characters at different moments, often out of chronological order, as if we’re dropping into a favorite long-running series. But unlike a television show, you linger on quieter, more marginal scenes, often with the characters alone in their thoughts. Could you speak about what draws you to those kinds of moments, and how they shape the characters you’re building? LR: I wanted to write a relationship where the reader felt like they were in on it. The ways people speak to each other when they’ve known each other for a long time can feel like intimacy, but they can also obfuscate intimacy, a way of not talking about what’s actually happening to them. I like doing something that feels a little thoughtless, where you simply feel the people: how they think, how they move through the world, how they interact with each other. They felt like very real characters to me, and I liked spending time with them. I like the idea of a Hollywood story that is very uncinematic. It’s an un-Hollywood love story. You don’t see the major climaxes or plot points. Even when Verity and Helen finally leave, you see them after they’ve already left. I wanted to write a relationship where the reader felt like they were in on it. What works for them is this very long friendship that is essentially romantic in nature. Sometimes they’re together, and when they’re not, they’re not—but I don’t think they ever feel that they’ve broken up or truly left each other. EJR: A recurring question in the book seems to be how we share space, both with other people and with ourselves. Verity, especially, is always searching for connection and authenticity. And Verity and Helen seem to have found that rare kind of connection with each other. LR: I don’t think they ever consider leaving each other. They operate under the assumption that they won’t like anyone else as much as they like each other. They’re different people, but there are certain things they see in a very similar way. Their relationship reminds me of the old Yiddish word landsman . It’s a term for meeting someone from your homeland, but it can also describe encountering someone who perceives the world the way you do—someone who simply sees things as you see them. EJR: Throughout Television , there’s a tension between reality and unreality, between what is true and what is performance. Sometimes performance is treated as artificial, and other times performance seems more real than reality itself. How do you think about performance in the book? LR: I was thinking a lot about how, in a very long relationship, you form the person you are around someone else, and it doesn’t feel like your complete self. It feels like one part of you, or one role that you’re playing. That doesn’t mean it isn’t real or true. It just feels very specific. That interested me, especially with an actor and a writer, because the story they’re telling about themselves is always going to be a kind of performance. If you’re making art because you have to, and you’re making what you love, then you just hope for the best. You can end up performing this role together over and over. It can be sweet, something you love and don’t want to lose, but it can also start to feel distant from yourself at times, like a mode you go into with someone else. To me, it feels like an inescapable paradox. The closer you get to someone, the more you create something slightly separate from yourself that you’re nurturing together. EJR: Verity seems to have this deep fixation on being good, and on what goodness even means. At one point, he tries to imagine a modern man who is kind, handsome, good at his job, and he comes up blank. Can you talk about Verity’s impulse toward goodness, and what you see as driving that need? LR: It’s something that confuses him. He’s drawn to things he perceives as pure or innocent. Sometimes he even makes a virtue out of things like not being conventionally beautiful. He describes his mother as spectacularly ugly, even dramatically ugly, and angry, but he attaches a certain kind of virtue to her that he doesn’t extend to his father, who was beautiful and simple and accepted things as they were. He also attaches virtue to a lack of success, especially monetary success. And then there’s the lottery. I don’t think he fully understands why he’s doing it as he’s doing it. It seems connected to guilt, a sense that he doesn’t deserve what he’s been given. Maybe he imagines that someone truly worthy will receive it, someone who deserves it. And when it’s just a random man who doesn’t fit his idea of worthiness, it’s depressing for him. I don’t think he fully understands his relationship to goodness and virtue, but there’s clearly a desire for it, a desire to feel that he’s good, that he’s honorable, that he’s doing things the right way.
